summary.text: Manganese nodules are lumps on the sea bottom made of layers of iron and manganese hydroxides built up around a core.
Their growth is one of the slowest known geological processes, about a centimetre over several million years, yet in places they cover more than 70% of the sea floor.
Because they are rich in nickel, copper, manganese and other rare metals, they have drawn growing interest as a mining resource.

paragraphs.heading: Metal lumps on the seabed
paragraphs.text: Manganese nodules, also known as polymetallic nodules, are mineral concretions found on the sea bottom. Each one is built of layers of iron and manganese hydroxides, wrapped one around another over a core. Depending on their makeup and on who is writing, they may also be called ferromanganese nodules. They rest on the sediment of the seabed, often partly or fully buried in it.

paragraphs.heading: Size and shape
paragraphs.text: Nodules range from specks seen only under a microscope to pellets over 20 centimetres across. Most are 3 to 10 cm wide, roughly the size of a hen's egg. Their surfaces can be smooth or rough, and are often knobby, a texture called botryoidal. Shapes run from round to flattened, sometimes stretched, or just irregular. The underside, sunk in sediment, is usually rougher than the top because it grows in a different way.

paragraphs.heading: Growing at a crawl
paragraphs.text: Nodule growth is among the slowest geological processes known, about a centimeter over several million years. How many nodules sit on a patch of seabed probably depends on how thick and stable a chemically active layer at the seabed is. Two styles of growth, called diagenetic and hydrogenetic, reflect growth with little oxygen and growth with oxygen present. Those in turn could relate to interglacial and glacial periods of climate.

paragraphs.heading: Where they turn up
paragraphs.text: Nodules occur in shallow seas such as the Baltic and in deep water such as the central Pacific, and even in lakes. They are thought to have formed since the deep oceans gained oxygen in the Ediacaran period, over 540 million years ago. They were first found in 1868 in the Kara Sea, part of the Arctic Ocean off Siberia, and the HMS Challenger expeditions of 1872 to 1876 found them in most of the world's oceans. In places they lie touching one another and cover more than 70% of the sea floor.

paragraphs.heading: The richest field
paragraphs.text: The biggest deposits, both in number of nodules and in metal content, are in the Clarion–Clipperton zone of the north central Pacific, roughly halfway between Hawaii and the Clipperton Islands. There they lie on huge abyssal plains between 4,000 and 6,000 m deep. In 1981, Alan A. Archer of the London Geological Museum put the total on the sea floor at 500 billion tons.

paragraphs.heading: Why miners are interested
paragraphs.text: Compared with the Earth's crust and the sediment around them, nodules are enriched in iron, manganese, heavy metals and rare earth elements. Ones from the sea tend to have more manganese relative to iron than ones from land. Their high share of nickel, copper, manganese and other rare metals has raised interest in mining them. Because they come in vast quantities and hold valuable metals, their deposits are seen as a possible economic resource.
